title: Trilce: Poem LX - My Patience Is Made of Wood
text:
My patience is made of wood,

deaf, vegetable.


Day that has been pure, child, useless,

that was born naked, the leagues

of your march go running over

your twelve extremities, that frowning fold

which afterward unthreads itself

into who knows what final swaddling clothes.


Constellated with hemispheres of clot,

beneath eternal unpublished Americas, your great plumage,

you divide yourself and leave me, without your ambiguous emotion,

without your knot of dreams, Sunday.


And my patience grows moth-eaten,

and I exclaim again: When will there come

the big-mouthed and mute Sunday of the sepulcher;

when will it come to carry this Saturday

of rags, this horrible suture

of the pleasure that begets us unwillingly,

and the pleasure that unEaRThs us!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the wooden patience, Sunday/Saturday structure, and the source's strange Tierra/Earth emphasis.

title: Trilce: Poem LXXII - Slow Conical Room, They Closed You, I Closed You
text:
Slow conical room, they closed you, I closed you,

although I loved you, you know it,

and today from whose hands will your keys hang?


From these walls we knocked down the last

scant pavilions that sang.

The greens have grown. I see laborers working,

the hills full of triumph.

And the month and a half gone by is enough

for a shroud, even more than enough.


Room of four entrances and not one exit,

today, since you have deep melancholy, I speak to you

in your six whole dialects.

Now I need not force you to be mine,

for never; now we will not leap

any other beloved wicket.


July was then nine. Love

counted in an odd sound. And sweetness

gave enough for the whole shroud, even more than enough.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the closed room's impossible entrances, dialects, shroud, and odd-numbered love.

title: Trilce: Poem LIII - Who Cries That Eleven Is Not Twelve
text:
Who cries that eleven is not twelve!

As if they had been bid up, they confront each other

two by two, the eleven times.


Brutal headbutt. Crowns appear

to listen,

but without crossing the eternal

three hundred sixty degrees, they appear

and explore in vain where both hands

hide the other bridge that is born to them

between truths and liturgical jokes.


The frontier returns to test

the two stones that cannot manage to occupy

one same lodging at one same time.

The frontier, the wandering baton, which remains

unchanged, equal, only

more itself at each high sprain.


You see what is without being able to be denied,

you see what we have to endure,

despite ourselves.

How much is oiled in elbows

that reach all the way to the mouth!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the clock-number dispute, frontier, baton, and body-mechanics of endurance.

title: Trilce: Poem XI - I Have Found a Girl
text:
I have found a girl

in the street, and she has embraced me.

X, disserted, whoever found her and finds her,

will not remember her.


This girl is my cousin. Today, touching

her waist, my hands entered her age

as into a pair of badly plastered sepulchers.

And through the same desolation she left,

                   delta toward the shadowy sun,

                   trilling between the two.


                   "I have married,"

she tells me. When what we did as children

in the dead aunt's house.

                   She has married.

                   She has married.


Late latitudinal years,

what true desire they gave us

to play at bulls, at yokes,

but everything of deceits, of candor, as it was.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the unsettling childhood-memory fracture and repeated 'She has married.'

title: The Black Cup
text:
Night is a cup of evil. A sharp whistle

from the guard pierces it, like a vibrating pin.

Listen, you, little harlot, how, if you have already gone,

the wave is still black and still makes me burn?


The Earth has coffin edges in the shadow.

Listen, you, little harlot, do not come back.


My flesh swims, swims

in the cup of shadow that still makes me ache;

my flesh swims in it,

as in a swampy woman's heart.


Astral ember... I have felt

dry rubs of clay

fall upon my diaphanous lotus.

Ah, woman! Because of you exists

flesh made of instinct. Ah, woman!


That is why, O black chalice, even though you have already gone,

I choke on dust;

and more desires to drink paw the ground in my flesh!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the source's pejorative address and dark erotic chalice imagery as historical poetic text.
